claims.text: The untreated refractory HEA has a single-phase or coarse-grained microstructure with limited mechanical performance under high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
Controlled subsolvus annealing induces a dual-phase microstructure in a refractory HEA.
The annealing treatment produces fine, coherent secondary-phase precipitates.
The annealing treatment leaves the coherent precipitates embedded in a nanocrystalline matrix.
Controlled subsolvus annealing can alternatively generate nano-twin boundaries in the refractory HEA.
The controlled thermal treatment facilitates stable nucleation of a secondary phase.
The resulting secondary phase generates continuous interfaces in the matrix.
The precipitate or twin interfaces impede dislocation glide.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the alloy's strength.
The proposed interfaces enhance toughness or ductility while they strengthen the alloy.
The precipitate or twin interfaces serve as stable sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
The interfaces trap irradiation-induced defects.
Defect trapping preserves irradiation stability.
The treated refractory HEA will have moderately higher yield strength than the untreated control.
The treated refractory HEA will have moderately higher ductility than the untreated control.
The treated refractory HEA may have moderately higher toughness than the untreated control.
The treated alloy will avoid significant phase-stability degradation during high-temperature exposure.
The treated alloy will avoid significant phase-stability degradation during irradiation exposure.
Excessive precipitate growth or grain coarsening caused by a poorly controlled annealing cycle will compromise mechanical and stability properties.
The predicted performance should hold under high-temperature and irradiation conditions representative of nuclear-reactor or aerospace environments.

contradictions.description: Nano-twins are offered as an alternative to nano-precipitates while the structure is still called dual-phase and the mechanism requires nucleation of a secondary phase. A twin-only branch would not itself constitute a second phase.

The predicted outcome permits improvement in ductility or toughness, whereas the falsification rule specifically requires improvements in yield strength and toughness. A yield-strength-plus-ductility improvement could therefore satisfy the prediction but still be classified as falsification.
